food.text: Between 450 BCE and 950 CE, pre-Columbian farming communities in the Amazon Basin created terra preta, a very dark and fertile soil. It was made by adding charcoal, bones, broken pottery, compost and manure to the low fertility Amazonian soil. The charcoal is stable and stays in the soil for thousands of years, binding and retaining minerals and nutrients.

On Marajo Island at the mouth of the Amazon, plant remains show a diet that relied heavily on small seed crops and small fish, which were cultivated or protected by indigenous peoples. Human remains show that these people limited their consumption of starchy root crops like manioc. Heavy tooth wear points to seeds, tree fruits and fish as their main foods.

Amazonians formed complex, large-scale societies, including chiefdoms. They may have used terra preta to make the land suitable for large-scale agriculture. The culture on the island of Marajó may have developed social stratification and supported a population of 100,000.
Açai and tucuma palms provided important supplements to the diet on Marajo Island, alongside seed crops and fish. The same trees were also used to make items such as baskets or canoes.

Several mounds on Marajo Island and in Bolivia have yielded radiocarbon dates as early as 1000 to 300 BC in their early levels. This suggests the first mounds were built in the Formative, the period when horticulture appears to become widespread for the first time.

Many terra preta soil structures are now thought to have formed under kitchen middens. Residues from food preparation, cooking fires, animal and fish bones and broken pottery built up near living quarters. Other terra preta was manufactured intentionally on larger scales.

Stone axes were the main agricultural technology at Marajo. Stone griddles, found at Teso Dos Bichos during Roosevelt's excavations, are very rare. Their rarity is another sign that root crops were absent from the diet.

Mounds on Marajo held malocas, Amazonian longhouses with several hearths lined up along the center, each likely serving one family. They had permanent cooking facilities made of baked clay and plastered floors that were frequently repaired. At Os Camutins, up to 20 structures were built atop one another.

Terra preta soils can reach 2 meters in depth. The soil is reported to regenerate itself at the rate of 1 centimeter per year. It was created by pre-Columbian farming communities between 450 BCE and 950 CE.

art.text: Excavations on Marajó island at the mouth of the Amazon River turned up sophisticated pottery. The pieces are large, and elaborately painted and incised with representations of plants and animals. They gave the first evidence that a complex society had existed on Marajó, where researchers have documented human activity as early as 1000 BC.

The Marajoara people made a wide range of objects beyond vessels. These included figurines, large statues, pubic covers, pendants, ear and lip jewelry, whistles and spindle whorls. Their pottery vessels came as urns, jars, bottles, cups, bowls, plates and dishes.

One of the best-known Marajoara forms is the globular urn, with painted and modeled decorations showing anthropomorphic figures (primates). Other urns combine painting, incisions, excisions and modeling to represent both human-like and animal figures.

The most common motif in Marajoara iconography is female imagery. Women appear as mythical ancestors, creators and cultural heroes, or in shamanistic roles with shamanistic power. These figures are typically found on ceramic artifacts, either pottery vessels or statues.

Marajoara potters also decorated vases with painted geometric patterns. Simpler forms included bowls, while more complex ones included double-base vases, funerary urns, small statues, plates and bowls on pedestals. The culture produced great diversity in shapes and decoration.

Stone objects were very rare on Marajó because the island has no source of suitable stone. The few that have been found suggest they were used as high-status items and gifts, or in craft production. This made stone unusual in a culture whose main medium was ceramics.
Marajoara craftspeople even made ceramic miniatures of tools. These included axes, mashers and hammers, and were made alongside whistles, spindle whorls and jewelry.

literature.text: Archaeological finds show that Mapuche culture existed in Chile and Argentina as early as 600 to 500 BC. Their culture relied on an oral tradition and lacked a writing system. A writing system for Mapudungun was developed only after the arrival of the Spanish.

In Guarani legend, Kerana, the beautiful daughter of Marangatu, was captured by Tau, the spirit of evil. Their seven sons were cursed by the high goddess Arasy, and all but one were born as hideous monsters.

Some of the lesser gods and even the original humans are forgotten in the verbal tradition of some areas. The seven sons of Tau and Kerana, however, were generally maintained in the legends, and some are still believed in, in rural areas today.

The Mapuche had no writing system before the Spanish arrived, and their language is now written with the Latin script. Writers still disagree on the alphabet, so the word for conversation or story can appear as gvxam, gytram, or ngütram.

science.text: The Amazon rainforest may be less wild than it looks. The BBC's Unnatural Histories presented evidence that it has been shaped by people for at least 11,000 years, through practices such as forest gardening and terra preta.

Terra preta is found over large areas of the Amazon forest and is now widely accepted as a product of indigenous soil management. This fertile soil allowed agriculture and silviculture in a previously hostile environment. Large portions of the rainforest are probably the result of centuries of human management.
In São Raimundo Nonato, agriculture has likely been practiced since at least 2,090 years ago. Cultivated plants had appeared even earlier in Minas Gerais, about 4,000 years ago.
Ondemar Dias is accredited with first discovering the Amazonian geoglyphs in 1977. Alceu Ranzi is credited with furthering their discovery after flying over Acre.
Amazonian pottery is older than agriculture, but elsewhere in Brazil the two appear together. The oldest pottery outside the Amazon dates back 3,000 years, also in the area of São Raimundo Nonato.

Brazilian archeologists link the appearance of pottery in these regions to sedentarism and agriculture. Pottery is difficult to transport and usually had the function of storing food, so it suggests people who stayed in one place.

culture.text: Since the 1970s, numerous geoglyphs have been discovered on deforested land in the Amazon, dating between AD 1 and 1250. They have furthered claims about Pre-Columbian civilizations in the region. They were an unexpected find in what was long assumed to be untouched forest.

Ondemar Dias is credited with first discovering the Amazon geoglyphs in 1977. Alceu Ranzi furthered their discovery after flying over Acre. Their work helped show that people had shaped the forest over long centuries.

Women are featured prominently in Marajoara art, portrayed as creators, lineage heroes or founders, and as figures with shamanistic powers. Households were matrilocal, and women were important in subsistence production. Interpretations of this society remain difficult.

Marajoara people placed their dead in urns and buried them in the mounds they also used for residence. For the elaborate urns, the flesh was cleared from the bones of significant individuals and the remains were placed in the urn, which was then topped with a bowl or platter. This suggests ancestor worship may have been very important. Their settlements were aligned east to west, consistent with an Amazonian cosmology that divides the universe by gender, with men related to the sun and women to the moon.
